common_name: Lucie Lemoine Clematis (Antique Double White Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring once frost danger has passed, burying the crown a few inches deep and shading the roots, and give immediate support since old-wood flowering begins on growth made the previous season.

directions: This old Lemoine-raised French heirloom produces densely overlapping, pure white double rosettes on the previous year's wood in late spring, sometimes followed by simpler single white flowers on fresh growth later in summer. Because the showy double blooms form only on old stems, prune lightly after flowering rather than cutting the whole plant back hard, removing just dead or weak wood. Give it cool, shaded roots with rich, well-drained soil and let the top growth climb into full sun on a wall, trellis, or obelisk. Its slow, modest vigor compared to modern hybrids suits a prized spot near a patio or entry where the old-fashioned flowers can be appreciated up close.

common_name: Prins Hendrik Clematis (Antique Mauve-Blue Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant deeply with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and roots kept cool and shaded, then provide a fence, obelisk, or wall support right away for this early-flowering, old-wood cultivar.

directions: One of the oldest Dutch-raised large-flowered hybrids still in circulation, this vigorous climber opens broad, flat, bright mauve-blue flowers with cream-yellow anthers, usually a few weeks earlier in the season than most large-flowered types. A light second flush of smaller flowers can appear on new growth in late summer. Prune only lightly in late winter since the main flush forms on stems grown the previous year, cutting back merely to remove dead or crossing wood. It performs best with its roots shaded and cool while the vines are trained into full sun on a sturdy support.

common_name: Mrs. James Mason Clematis (Mauve-Pink Large-Flowered Clematis)

planting.note: Plant with the crown set a couple of inches below grade and roots shaded from direct sun, training stems onto a trellis or fence as soon as new growth appears.

directions: Bred by Barry Fretwell at Peveril Clematis Nursery in Devon, England, and a long-standing Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit holder, this reliable large-flowered climber bears broad, deep mauve-pink blooms with slightly wavy sepal edges and contrasting stamens over a long summer season. It flowers on both old and new wood, so it tolerates either light pruning in late winter to shape it or a harder cutback if the plant becomes bare at the base. Rich, well-drained soil and a cool root zone help it establish quickly, while the twining stems should be given a fence, obelisk, or shrub to scramble through in full sun. Its dependable repeat bloom and tidy flower form have kept it popular with gardeners long after flashier modern hybrids arrived.

common_name: Blue Light Clematis (Double Violet-Blue Patio Clematis)

planting.note: Grow in a large container or border spot with roots shaded, giving a small obelisk or trellis right away since this compact cultivar is bred to climb only modestly.

directions: This patented compact patio cultivar, a sport of 'Mrs. Cholmondeley', opens fully double, violet-blue rosette flowers on the previous year's wood in late spring, then continues with simpler single blue flowers on new growth into summer. Its shorter, restrained habit compared to traditional large-flowered hybrids makes it well suited to a container, small trellis, or mailbox post rather than a tall wall or arbor. Prune only lightly after the first flush to preserve the old wood that produces the showy doubles, removing just weak or dead stems. Keep the roots cool and shaded with mulch or a companion planting while the foliage and flowers enjoy full sun.

planting.note: Set the crown a couple of inches below soil level with roots shaded and cool, then provide a fence or trellis immediately for this early, old-wood-flowering cultivar.

directions: Bred by Tage Lundell in Sweden in 1960 and introduced to Britain by Treasures of Tenbury in 1969, this large-flowered hybrid opens pearly white blooms with a soft pink blush, giving the flower a gentle two-toned glow reminiscent of early morning light. It blooms earliest on stems carried over from the previous season, so prune lightly in late winter rather than cutting hard, taking out only dead or crowded growth. A cool, shaded root zone paired with full sun on the climbing stems keeps flower color from fading too quickly in hot weather. Its gentle pastel tone makes it a useful companion for pairing with deeper purple or red clematis on the same support.

planting.note: Plant deeply with the crown shaded and cool and give a trellis, fence, or obelisk right away so twining leaf stalks can grip support as new growth lengthens.

directions: This hardy large-flowered climber produces broad, rich purple-blue flowers with contrasting magenta central bands and golden anthers across a long summer season. Because it can flower on both old and new wood, it accepts either a light shaping prune in late winter or a harder renewal cut if growth becomes sparse near the base. Rich, humus-amended soil with a cool, shaded root zone and full sun on the vines encourages the strongest bloom production. It combines well with climbing roses or other vigorous shrubs that can offer extra support and structure.
